1.title: ADM REQUIREMENTS MANAGEMENT
1.text: Welcome to Module 7. Throughout this course, every time we've drawn the ADM wheel, there's been something sitting right in the middle — Requirements Management. We've mentioned it again and again, but now it gets its own focused treatment. It's the continuous activity at the center of the ADM, connected to every phase. It's also a reliable source of exam questions, because it behaves in a way that surprises people. So let's understand exactly what it is, and just as importantly, what it isn't.

1.title: Module Overview & Learning Objectives
1.text: Here's the plan. You'll understand why Requirements Management is drawn at the center of the ADM. You'll state its objectives, and you'll learn the crucial distinction between what it does and what it does not do. You'll meet the Architecture Requirements Specification and the Requirements Repository, where requirements live. You'll understand the Requirements Impact Assessment. And you'll walk through the steps of the process. If you take one idea from this whole module, make it this: Requirements Management manages the flow of requirements — it doesn't resolve them itself.

1.title: Why It's at the Center
1.text: Let's start with placement. Why is Requirements Management drawn in the center of the wheel rather than as a step around the rim? Because requirements are identified, stored, and fed in and out across every single ADM phase. Putting it in the center is a deliberate visual statement: it's connected to all phases simultaneously, rather than being one stop on a sequence. And it's a dynamic, continuous process — requirements don't sit still; they're constantly arriving and changing. So the foundational idea is that Requirements Management is continuous, operating throughout the entire ADM, and it's never truly finished.

1.title: A Phase That Is Not a Sequential Phase
1.text: Here's a subtlety that the exam genuinely enjoys testing. TOGAF officially calls this the Requirements Management phase — but it does not run in sequence the way Phases A through H do. Instead, it operates in parallel with every other phase, all the time. Every phase both populates it with new requirements and draws existing requirements from it. So you have this slightly odd situation: it's labelled a "phase," but it behaves as a continuous central process, not a sequential one. If a question implies Requirements Management runs once in a fixed slot in the sequence, that's the trap — it runs throughout.

1.title: The Objectives
1.text: Requirements Management has three objectives, and they're worth holding as a trio. First, to sustain the Requirements Management process across all relevant ADM phases — to keep it running, continuously. Second, to manage the architecture requirements identified during any execution of the ADM — whether a full cycle or a single phase. And third, to ensure that the relevant requirements are available for use by each phase as that phase executes — so the right requirements are in the right hands at the right time. Sustain, manage, make available — that's the clean three-part summary of what Requirements Management sets out to achieve.

1.title: What It Does NOT Do
1.text: Now the single most important slide in this module — what Requirements Management does not do. It does not, itself, dispose of, address, or prioritize requirements. Read that again, because it's counterintuitive. You'd expect the requirements process to be where requirements get decided — but in TOGAF, that disposition happens within the relevant ADM phases, A through H. Requirements Management's job is purely to manage the flow: to capture requirements, store them, and route them to the right phase, where they're actually resolved. So the mantra to memorize is: Requirements Management manages; the phases resolve. The exam tests this distinction directly and often, so make it second nature.

1.title: The Architecture Requirements Specification
1.text: Let's look at where requirements are written down. The Architecture Requirements Specification documents the quantitative requirements that the architecture must meet — the measurable criteria. You'll recognize it as the companion to the Architecture Definition Document, which we met earlier: the ADD is the qualitative description of the architecture, while the Requirements Specification is the quantitative set of requirements it must satisfy. Requirements are identified and refined within the phases, but they're recorded here. So keep the pairing straight: the Requirements Specification holds the measurable requirements; the ADD holds the architecture description itself.

1.title: The Requirements Repository
1.text: Alongside the specification document is the Requirements Repository. This holds all the authorized architecture requirements for the enterprise — it's the single source of truth that every phase reads from and writes to. Having one repository, rather than scattered lists in different teams' spreadsheets, is what prevents requirements from being lost, duplicated, or contradicted. And it's not a standalone thing — the Requirements Repository is one component of the wider Architecture Repository, which we'll explore fully in the next module. For now: all requirements flow through a single, governed Requirements Repository.

1.title: The Requirements Impact Assessment
1.text: When requirements change — and they always do — TOGAF uses a specific tool to handle it: the Requirements Impact Assessment. This assessment evaluates the effect of new or changed requirements on the current phase and on the phases already completed. Its purpose is to steer the architecture team — to show clearly what needs to be revisited or reworked in light of the change. It's a key output because it's what keeps the architecture internally consistent as requirements evolve, rather than letting changes quietly break earlier decisions. So remember the definition: the Requirements Impact Assessment captures the impact of changed requirements on the architecture work.

1.title: The Requirements Management Steps
1.text: Let's walk the steps of the process. Step one: identify requirements — typically by analyzing how business goals can be met through value streams, business scenarios, and the like — and document them. Step two: establish baseline requirements, which means determining priorities and confirming stakeholder agreement to those priorities. Step three: monitor the baseline requirements over time. Step four: identify new and changed requirements — adding, removing, or modifying them, and re-assessing priorities. And step five: record the changed priorities and generate the Requirements Impact Assessment to steer the team. So the flow is: identify, baseline, monitor, identify changes, assess impact. A continuous loop, not a one-time pass.

1.title: How Requirements Are Discovered
1.text: Where do requirements actually come from? They're typically identified by analyzing how the business's goals and objectives can be met — and TOGAF lists several lenses for that analysis. You can look through value streams, asking what each stage of value delivery requires. You can use business scenarios, which we met back in Phase A. You can consider user experiences. And you can look at management information needs. Of these, business scenarios are the headline technique for discovering requirements, especially in Phases A and B. So if a question asks how requirements are discovered, business scenarios should be the first thing that comes to mind.

1.title: Requirements Flow Through the ADM
1.text: Let's visualize the whole thing. Picture Requirements Management as a hub in the center, with spokes radiating out to every ADM phase, as the diagram shows. Each phase raises new requirements and consumes existing ones — so requirements flow both into the hub and out of it. When a requirement changes, that change is routed through the hub, assessed via the Requirements Impact Assessment, and then directed back into whichever phase needs to act on it. This hub-and-spoke image is exactly the mental model the exam expects you to have. If you can picture the hub connected to all nine phases, you understand Requirements Management.

1.title: Inputs to Requirements Management
1.text: Briefly, the inputs. Requirements Management consumes a populated Architecture Repository, the Organizational Model for Enterprise Architecture, and the Tailored Architecture Framework — the same foundational inputs the phases use. It also takes in the Statement of Architecture Work and the Architecture Vision, which give it context for this cycle. And of course it takes in the architecture requirements themselves, along with any Requirements Impact Assessment. The pattern to notice is that Requirements Management draws on the same foundational inputs as the phases, plus the live requirements it exists to manage. Nothing exotic — just the standard architecture context, plus the requirements.

1.title: Why Requirements Management Matters
1.text: Let's step back and ask why this matters. All architecture work is driven by requirements — they're the justification for every design decision you make. But requirements change constantly, as the business shifts and stakeholders learn more. Without disciplined management of those changes, the architecture quietly drifts away from what's actually needed. And a single, governed repository is what prevents requirements from conflicting with each other or simply getting lost. The crux, as TOGAF frames it, is the ability to deal with changing requirements. Architecture isn't hard because requirements are hard to write down; it's hard because they keep moving. Requirements Management is how you cope.

1.title: Conflicts & Prioritization
1.text: A word on conflicts and prioritization, because this clarifies the "manages versus resolves" distinction. Changed requirements can enter through any route, at any time — there's no single gate. Requirements Management ensures that any conflicts those changes create are identified and then managed through the phases to a successful conclusion. But notice who actually does the prioritizing: it's the architects responsible for the current phase, together with the relevant stakeholders. Requirements Management surfaces the conflict and routes it; the phases and stakeholders resolve and prioritize it. Again, the same theme — RM coordinates, the phases decide.

1.title: Requirements Management vs the Phases
1.text: Let's put Requirements Management and the ADM phases side by side, because the contrast nails the concept. Requirements Management's role is to manage the flow; the phases' role is to resolve and implement. Requirements Management runs continuously, in the center; the phases run in sequence and iteration around the rim. Does Requirements Management dispose of requirements? No. Do the phases? Yes, within the phase. And the outputs differ: Requirements Management produces things like the Impact Assessment and an updated repository, while the phases produce actual architecture content. Manage versus resolve, continuous versus sequential — that comparison is the heart of every exam question here.

1.title: Common Exam Traps
1.text: Let's clear the traps. One: "Requirements Management addresses and prioritizes requirements itself" — no, the phases do that; RM manages the flow. Two: "it runs once, like a normal phase" — no, it's continuous, at the center. Three: "requirements live in many scattered lists" — no, there's a single Requirements Repository. And four: "the Requirements Impact Assessment is just about cost" — no, it's about the impact of changed requirements on the architecture work as a whole. The most-tested idea by far is the first one — that RM manages but does not resolve. If you remember nothing else, remember that.

1.title: Key Numbers & Quick Facts (Cheat Sheet)
1.text: Your Requirements Management cheat-sheet. Its position in the ADM is the center, and it runs continuously. It has three objectives — sustain, manage, make available. Does it resolve requirements? No — the phases do. Its key document is the Architecture Requirements Specification. Its key store is the Requirements Repository. Its change tool is the Requirements Impact Assessment. Its headline discovery technique is business scenarios. And its steps run: identify, baseline, monitor, change, assess. A compact card that covers essentially every recall question this topic can produce.

1.title: Module Summary
1.text: Let's recap. Requirements Management is the continuous center of the ADM, connected to every phase. It manages the flow of requirements, but it does not dispose of, address, or prioritize them — the phases do that. Requirements are recorded in the Architecture Requirements Specification and stored in the single Requirements Repository. The Requirements Impact Assessment evaluates the effect of changed requirements and steers the team. And discovery draws on business scenarios, value streams, and user experiences. Short module, but a high-value one — the "manages, doesn't resolve" point alone is worth guarding carefully.

1.title: Where This Fits in the Course
1.text: Let's take stock of where we are. With this module, we've now covered the full ADM — all nine phases plus the central process that ties them together. From here, the course turns to the supporting structures that make the method work. Next up, Module 8, is the Enterprise Continuum and the Architecture Repository — the home and classification scheme for all the assets we keep producing. After that come the Content Framework, partitioning, stakeholders, governance, and the reference models. And there's a neat link: requirements live inside the Repository, which makes Module 8 a natural next step.

1.title: Quick Self-Check
1.text: A quick self-check before the questions. From memory: can you explain why Requirements Management is drawn at the center of the wheel? Can you state the one thing it does not do? Can you name both the document and the store where requirements are kept? And can you define the Requirements Impact Assessment? If that "manages versus resolves" point still feels even a little fuzzy, go back and re-watch slide six — it's the conceptual core of the whole module, and the one the exam leans on hardest.

1.title: One Mental Model to Keep
1.text: Let me leave you with one mental model that makes this stick. Think of Requirements Management as the air-traffic control of the ADM. Air-traffic control doesn't fly the planes — the pilots do. In the same way, Requirements Management doesn't resolve the requirements — the phases do. What air-traffic control does is track, route, and coordinate every aircraft so nothing collides and everything reaches its destination safely. That's exactly Requirements Management's job with requirements. Manage the flow, don't pilot the planes. It's a handy hook for recalling the core distinction under exam pressure.

1.title: Bridge to Module 8
1.text: So where next? We've seen that requirements, architectures, and solutions are all constantly being produced — and they all need a home and a way of being classified so they can be found and reused. That home is the Architecture Repository, and the classification scheme is the Enterprise Continuum. Those are the subjects of Module 8. And here's the connecting thread: the Requirements Repository we just discussed is one component of that larger Architecture Repository. Let's go see the whole structure.

1.title: Practice Question 1
1.text: Question 1. Where is Requirements Management positioned in the ADM, and how often does it operate? Pause to consider your answer. The correct answer is B. At the center, operating continuously throughout all phases Requirements Management sits at the center of the ADM and operates continuously, connected to every phase. It is drawn in the middle of the cycle precisely because it is not a sequential step.

1.title: Practice Question 2
1.text: Question 2. Which statement correctly describes what Requirements Management does? Pause to consider your answer. The correct answer is B. It manages the flow of requirements; the disposition/resolution happens within the ADM phases Requirements Management manages the flow of requirements — capturing, storing, and routing them — but it does not dispose of, address, or prioritize them itself. That resolution happens within the relevant ADM phases.

1.title: Practice Question 3
1.text: Question 3. What is the purpose of a Requirements Impact Assessment? Pause to consider your answer. The correct answer is B. To assess the effect of new or changed requirements on the architecture work and steer the team A Requirements Impact Assessment evaluates how new or changed requirements affect the current and prior ADM phases, steering the architecture team on what must be revisited to keep the architecture consistent.

1.title: Practice Question 4
1.text: Question 4. In which document are the quantitative architecture requirements recorded? Pause to consider your answer. The correct answer is B. The Architecture Requirements Specification The Architecture Requirements Specification records the quantitative, measurable requirements the architecture must meet. It is the companion to the Architecture Definition Document, which holds the qualitative architecture description.

1.title: Practice Question 5
1.text: Question 5. Requirements are typically discovered by analyzing how business goals can be met through which of the following? Pause to consider your answer. The correct answer is A. Value streams, business scenarios, and user experiences Requirements are typically identified by analyzing how business goals and objectives can be met through value streams, business scenarios, user experiences, and management information needs. Business Scenarios (used in Phases A and B) are the headline discovery technique.
